rewrites.summary: This division was covered by the dedicated country dossier, which identified no deviation from the national position material enough to score separately (±0.02); it is therefore assessed at the national score. The national framework a visitor stands under is protective in form: the constitution bars sexual-orientation discrimination; after a 2005 judgment of the constitutional court, the elected national legislature legalised same-sex marriage in November 2006, so marriage-based partner status is recognised for a trans visitor travelling with a spouse; and sex status can be changed in the population registry — and therefore on identity documents and passports — on proof of medical treatment such as hormone therapy, without requiring surgery (the 2003 alteration-of-sex-description law). The landmark ruling of 10 November 2025 in the trans-inmate case affirms gender-affirming healthcare as part of adequate medical care, although the case concerns a correctional facility in another division, so the national correctional policy is the correct frame for this division rather than any division-specific finding.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: National litigation flux: the 10 November 2025 trans-inmate ruling, welcomed by the national preventive mechanism's statement of 14 November 2025, affirms gender-affirming healthcare as part of adequate medical care — a national precedent colouring, but not changing, this division's assessment; the freshness review records that the case is a facility case in another division that was initially misattributed to this record, the national correctional policy being the correct frame. The sources record no neighbour comparison for this division.

The dossier records no division-specific cultural-role, birth-register or resident-discrimination data for this division beyond that national care-access picture.

National preventive mechanism media statement (14 November 2025): welcomes the 10 November 2025 ruling in the trans-inmate case; describes the monitoring mandate over places of deprivation of liberty, the inmate's account (initially allowed to express her gender, later restricted from feminine clothing and make-up, misgendered, denied prescribed hormone therapy, with the service arguing it was cosmetic), and the court's finding that gender-affirming healthcare forms part of adequate medical treatment under the constitution.

Encyclopaedia overview of rights in the parent nation: the 1996 constitution was the world's first to expressly bar sexual-orientation discrimination; a December 2005 judgment of the constitutional court pushed the elected national legislature to legalise same-sex marriage, passed in November 2006; a 2003 law allows a person to change sex status in the population registry — and therefore on identity documents and passports — on proof of medical treatment such as hormone therapy, without requiring surgery. Gender-affirming care is concentrated in the main cities, so transgender people in provinces like this one must travel long distances to reach it, with private treatment costing hundreds of thousands of rands and long public waiting lists; this grounds this division's at-national-score assessment in the national framework a visitor stands under.

rewrites.summary: This division was covered by the dedicated country dossier, which identified no deviation from the national position material enough to score separately (±0.02); it is therefore assessed at the national score, with the national mechanisms the sources document applying here unchanged. For a trans visitor the operative exposure is custodial: prison placement follows the legal sex on identity documents (under the criminal-procedure code), so trans women whose legal gender is marked male — the vast majority — are placed in men's facilities. The national controller of places of deprivation of liberty reports that transgender detainees, overwhelmingly women, are the group that suffers most in prison, and the national preventive mechanism documents persistent serious violations of trans detainees' rights in adult prisons.

The sources record no policy turbulence, litigation flux or neighbour comparison for this division.
